newsitem.title: USA: Boeing gave up little in deal with EU - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Boeing gave up little in deal with EU - analysts.

text.p: Boeing Co. will feel little impact from concessions made to win European Union approval for its plan to acquire McDonnell Douglas Corp., industry analysts and company executives said on Wednesday.

Wall Street welcomed news of the agreement with the European Commission, driving up Boeing stock $2.8125 to $59.1875 on the New York Stock Exchange, and raising the value of the merger to more than $16 billion. McDonnell Douglas stock rose $4.50 to $76.25 in consolidated NSE trading.

"I don't think they gave up a thing," said analyst Paul Nisbet of JSA Research. "It's just some technicalities as a sop to the Europeans, who had gotten out of hand with their rhetoric and now have a half-graceful way to get out of this thing."

Boeing Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit said at a news conference the company's concessions would have little if any impact on the increased profits the company expects after it closes the merger next week.
"I believe that given this agreement we can have -- if not zero impact -- minimal impact on the bottom line," Condit said at a news conference.

He and McDonnell Douglas President and Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher said they expected their shareholders to approve the deal at separate meetings on Friday, clearing the way for the deal to close on Aug. 1.

In the most visible concession of Boeing's 11th-hour deal, the Seattle-based manufacturer agreed not to sign any exclusive airline sales deals for 10 years and to scrap sole-supplier contracts with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Continental Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc.

But officials of American and Continental quickly said the move would make no difference in their purchase plans, and analysts pointed out that firm orders from the airlines would make it difficult for Boeing's European rival Airbus Industrie to win back any of that business.

"By holding that obvious card until the last minute, Boeing was able to get a very good deal for themselves," said Jon Kutler of Quarterdeck Investment Partners, an investment bank for aerospace companies.

Boeing also agreed to license out commercial technology obtained from government contracts, operate McDonnell Douglas' commercial aviation division as a separate legal entity for 10 years, and refrain from abusing its dominant position with suppliers or customers.
But Condit said that any technology licenses would be "very limited" and that the other concessions would have no impact on how Boeing plans to operate the combined business.

While EC officials trying to ensure future competition focused on the commercial aviation market, which will be left with only two significant players, company executives and analysts said the main impact of the deal will be to diversify Boeing further into defence and space.

Analyst Peter Jacobs of brokerage Ragen MacKenzie estimated the combined company would generate $49 billion in revenue this year, of which 61 percent would come from commercial jets. Without the acquisition Boeing would have $34.7 billion in revenue this year, with 76 percent coming from the commercial side.

Jacobs estimated the deal would boost Boeing earnings per share about 13 percent this year, but he said the merger could be dilutive by 1999 because of McDonnell Douglas' heavy reliance on less-profitable government business.

Analysts said Boeing's main challenge would be to integrate McDonnell Douglas operations as it continues to speed up production to meet rising airline demand, a process that has been squeezing profit margins.
And analysts said Airbus needs to become more aggressive in developing new models and generating profits so it ultimately could come to the public market for financing.
